explanations.answer: Cross over armed ahead of their brothers
explanations.explanation: Moses, Israel's leader, tells these men, "All your men of valor are to cross over, armed for battle, ahead of your brothers, the Israelites." Their own land is already settled, but their brothers don't have theirs yet. So these men go first. That's like getting your own keys and then being asked to help carry everybody else's couch.

explanations.answer: Stay behind and guard their new cities
explanations.explanation: Close, because somebody does stay in those cities. But it's not the men of valor. Moses says their wives, children and livestock may remain there. The fighting men are told to cross over armed.

explanations.answer: Build a wall along the Jordan River
explanations.explanation: No wall shows up anywhere in this passage, friend. The Jordan River is described as bordering that land (Deuteronomy 3:17), and Moses says, "All your men of valor are to cross over, armed for battle, ahead of your brothers, the Israelites." His order is about crossing the river, not building along it. Nobody gets handed a trowel in this passage.

That's not what Moses says. He commands the men of valor to cross over, armed for battle. About the wives, children and livestock, he says they "…may remain in the cities I have given you…" So staying is allowed for them, not crossing required.

That's right. Moses commands the men of valor to cross over, armed for battle. But he says the wives, children and livestock "…may remain in the cities I have given you…" He even adds, "…I know that you have much livestock…" The families and herds are allowed to stay put.

Yes. Moses says the families and herds may remain "…until the LORD gives rest to your brothers as He has to you, and they too have taken possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving them across the Jordan." These tribes already have rest, and their brothers are still waiting for theirs. Moses ties it to two things, the rest and the brothers taking possession, and he doesn't name a day.
I get it, they do have a lot of livestock. But the word in the verse isn't wealth. Moses says the LORD gives "…rest to your brothers as He has to you…" Nobody is being handed a bank account here.

Wisdom is a good thing to want, but it isn't the word in this verse. Moses says the LORD gives "…rest to your brothers as He has to you…" The brothers are waiting on rest and on land. A smarter brain isn't on the list.

explanations.answer: Return to the land Moses gave him
explanations.explanation: Moses says, "Then each of you may return to the possession I have given you." First the brothers take possession of the land the LORD is giving them across the Jordan. After that, these men go home to what they already have. I'd bet the walk home feels pretty good.

explanations.answer: Pick new land on the west side
explanations.explanation: No, friend. The land west of the Jordan is for their brothers, who are waiting to take possession of it. Moses tells these men they may return "…to the possession I have given you." They already have their land, so there's nothing to pick.

explanations.answer: Stay on to serve under Joshua
explanations.explanation: Joshua does show up in this passage, but not for this. Moses tells these men that after their brothers have taken possession of their land, "…each of you may return to the possession I have given you." Nothing in that verse says these men stay on under anyone. Joshua gets his own word from Moses a verse later.

explanations.answer: The LORD Himself will fight for him
explanations.explanation: Moses tells Joshua, "Do not be afraid of them, for the LORD your God Himself will fight for you." Joshua is the one Moses is speaking to, and the kingdoms are ones he's "…about to enter." Moses also reminds him, "Your own eyes have seen all that the LORD your God has done to these two kings." So the reason isn't how strong Joshua is. It's who is fighting.

explanations.answer: Israel's army is far bigger than theirs
explanations.explanation: Moses never compares the armies, friend. The reason he gives is that "…the LORD your God Himself will fight for you." He points Joshua to what the LORD has already done to the two kings, not to how many soldiers Israel has.

Nothing here says they've surrendered. Moses calls them kingdoms Joshua is "…about to enter." and tells him not to be afraid of them. The reason he gives is that "…the LORD your God Himself will fight for you." That's the whole reason on the table.

explanations.answer: To cross over and see the good land
explanations.explanation: Moses asks, "Please let me cross over and see the good land beyond the Jordan…" He also names the pleasant hill country and Lebanon. Right before that, he calls the LORD's works great and mighty. I think wanting to see the land after all of that is a very human thing.

explanations.answer: To defeat one more king in battle
explanations.explanation: One more battle? Not this time, friend. Moses has just reminded Joshua what the LORD did to "…these two kings." (Deuteronomy 3:21). But what he asks for is something else: "Please let me cross over and see the good land beyond the Jordan…" (Deuteronomy 3:25). No sword in sight, just a request to see the land.

explanations.answer: To see the face of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Not here, friend. Moses calls the LORD great and powerful and asks something different: "Please let me cross over and see the good land beyond the Jordan…" His request is about the land, not about seeing the LORD's face.
That's the opposite of what the LORD says. He tells Moses, "That is enough… Do not speak to Me again about this matter." Moses doesn't get a later date to ask again. The LORD closes the subject.
That's right. The LORD tells Moses, "That is enough… Do not speak to Me again about this matter." There's no "ask me later" in that. The subject is closed, and Moses is told to stop bringing it up.

explanations.answer: Look over the land in every direction
explanations.explanation: The LORD tells Moses, "Go to the top of Pisgah and look to the west and north and south and east. See the land with your own eyes…" That's four directions to look. Moses can't walk in, but he does get to see the land with his own eyes.

explanations.answer: Pray for the people camped below
explanations.explanation: Praying is a good thing to do on a mountain. But that isn't the order here. The LORD tells Moses to go to the top of Pisgah and look to the west, north, south and east. He's sent up there to see the land with his own eyes.

explanations.answer: Build an altar out of the stones
explanations.explanation: The LORD says nothing about an altar here, friend. His order for the top of Pisgah is to look to the west, north, south and east. No stones, no building, just Moses and the view.

Yes. The LORD says, "See the land with your own eyes, for you will not cross this Jordan." Moses gets to look but not to walk in. I think that's a heavy thing to hear, and it's okay to let it be heavy.

The text says the opposite. The LORD tells Moses, "See the land with your own eyes, for you will not cross this Jordan." Moses will look at the land from Pisgah but won't go in. I think that one stings.

The LORD says, "But commission Joshua, encourage him, and strengthen him…" Moses won't be crossing, but he still has a job to do for the man who will. I think that's a kind way to hand things off. He gets to cheer on the guy who will cross ahead of the people.

Writing things down is a fine job, but it isn't the order here. The LORD tells Moses to "…commission Joshua, encourage him, and strengthen him…" The order in this passage is about a person, not a notebook.

Blessing every tribe by name? That's a big job, friend, and I'd have been up all night reading the list. Not in this passage, though. Moses did give out land to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh earlier, but the LORD's last order here is about one man: "But commission Joshua, encourage him, and strengthen him…" (Deuteronomy 3:28). I think that's a handoff worth remembering.

That's the word. The LORD says Joshua "…will cross over ahead of the people and enable them to inherit the land that you will see." Moses is the one who will see the land, and Joshua is the one who leads them into it. Moses sees it, Joshua helps Israel receive it.
Guarding sounds like a fair guess for a leader. But the LORD says Joshua will "…enable them to inherit the land that you will see." The word is inherit. It's a gift they receive.

Rebuilding is a fair guess for a leader, but it isn't the word in this verse. The LORD says Joshua will "…enable them to inherit the land that you will see." The word is inherit. It's something the people receive.
